items: 1Identify the groups of carbohydrates — monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides, and how they are classified and named.
2Explain the functions of carbohydrates — as energy sources, energy stores, and providers of physical structure and strength to organisms.
3Understand some tests for carbohydrates — Molisch's, Bial's, Seliwanoff's, Benedict's, Fehling's, and Barfoed's tests.

blocks.x: Core definitions

Carbohydrate Polyhydroxy carbonyl compounds and their derivatives (hemiacetals, hemiketals, acetals, ketals). Molecular formula: Cx(H2O)y. They are the primary form of stored energy and the metabolic precursors of virtually all other biomolecules.
Monosaccharide A simple sugar — the simplest carbohydrate, containing a single sugar unit. General formula (CH2O)n, n = 3 to 7.
Oligosaccharide A chain of 2–10 simple sugars joined by glycosidic bonds; disaccharides are the simplest oligosaccharides.
Polysaccharide A chain of more than 10 simple sugars (glycans); classified as homopolysaccharides (one type of monosaccharide) or heteropolysaccharides (more than one type).

Plants produce carbohydrates through photosynthesis; they are the essential source of energy for animals. A healthy diet should contain both complex carbohydrates (starch, cellulose) and simple sugars (fructose, sucrose) — but large amounts of simple sugars, principally sucrose, promote obesity and tooth decay.
Monosaccharide→ Oligosaccharide (2–10)→ Polysaccharide (>10)
How monosaccharides get their names

c: D- or L- isomeric form, based on the reference carbon

blocks.x: Because monosaccharides contain many hydroxyl groups, they are sometimes called polyhydroxy aldehydes or polyhydroxy ketones.
Simple sugars
Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates — a single (mono-) sugar (saccharide) unit, composed of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.
Aldoses vs. ketoses
Aldose
Carries an aldehyde group (CHO) at carbon-1. Example: D-glyceraldehyde (the simplest aldotriose), D-glucose (an aldohexose).
Ketose
Carries a ketone group (C=O) at carbon-2. Example: dihydroxyacetone (the simplest ketotriose), D-fructose (a ketohexose).

blocks.title: Family tree of the aldoses (from glyceraldehyde)

blocks.x: Each addition of a carbon to D-glyceraldehyde doubles the number of possible stereoisomers:

items: Aldotriose (3C): D-glyceraldehyde
Aldotetroses (4C): D-erythrose, D-threose
Aldopentoses (5C): D-ribose, D-arabinose, D-xylose, D-lyxose
Aldohexoses (6C): D-allose, D-altrose, D-glucose, D-mannose, D-gulose, D-idose, D-galactose, D-talose

blocks.title: Family tree of the ketoses (from dihydroxyacetone)

items: Ketotriose: triulose (dihydroxyacetone)
Ketotetrose: tetrulose (D-erythrulose)
Ketopentoses: pentulose (D-ribulose, D-xylulose)
Ketohexoses: hexulose (D-psicose, D-fructose, D-sorbose, D-tagatose)

blocks.x: General naming pattern: keto…ose → …ulose (e.g. ketohexose → hexulose).
Hemiacetals, hemiketals & anomers
Monosaccharides exist in equilibrium between open-chain and cyclic forms. An alcohol reacting with an aldehyde forms a hemiacetal; an alcohol reacting with a ketone forms a hemiketal.

In D-glucose, the C-1 aldehyde reacts intramolecularly with the C-5 hydroxyl to give a six-membered ring (a pyranose) — α-D-glucopyranose or β-D-glucopyranose. In D-fructose, the C-2 keto group reacts with the C-5 hydroxyl to give a five-membered ring (a furanose) — α- or β-D-fructofuranose.
The new stereocentre created at C-1 (or C-2 for ketoses) generates two anomers, α and β, shown in Haworth or Fischer projection formulas.
Seven derivative forms of monosaccharides

items: Sugar acids: formed by oxidation of sugars. Oxidation of D-glucose at C-1 gives D-gluconic acid (which equilibrates with D-δ-gluconolactone); oxidation at C-6 gives D-glucuronic acid; oxidation at both C-1 and C-6 gives D-glucaric acid.
Sugar alcohols: formed by reduction of the carbonyl group. Examples: D-glucitol (sorbitol), D-mannitol, D-xylitol, D-glycerol, myo-inositol, D-ribitol.

blocks.title: 3–5. Deoxy sugars, sugar esters & amino sugars

items: Deoxy sugars: a hydroxyl is replaced by hydrogen. Examples: 2-deoxy-α-D-ribose (in DNA), α-L-rhamnose, α-L-fucose.
Sugar esters: phosphate esters carry intermediates through metabolism, e.g. α-D-glucose-1-phosphate, α-D-fructose-1,6-bisphosphate, and adenosine-5'-triphosphate (ATP).
Amino sugars: a hydroxyl is replaced by an amino group. Examples: β-D-glucosamine and β-D-galactosamine, found in the polysaccharides of cell membranes.
Acetals/ketals: a hemiacetal (or hemiketal) reacts with a further alcohol, releasing water, to form an acetal (or ketal).

Glycosides: the anomeric hydroxyl of a cyclic sugar reacts with an –OH of another molecule, forming a glycosidic bond — e.g. methyl-α-D-glucoside and methyl-β-D-glucoside. Glycosidic bonds are what link sugar units together in oligo- and polysaccharides.

blocks.x: Biologically important monosaccharides

GLUCOSEDextrose / blood sugar — C6H12O6, an aldohexose; the most essential sugar in the human body, broken down in glycolysis; controlled by insulin and glucagon. Normal blood glucose: 3.9–5.5 mmol/L, highest after a meal (postprandial).

FRUCTOSELevulose / fruit sugar — the sweetest simple sugar, abundant in honey, corn syrup and sweet fruits. A ketohexose; the C-2 keto group and C-5 hydroxyl form an intramolecular hemiketal on cyclisation.

GALACTOSEMilk-sugar component — a hexose that combines with glucose to form lactose. β-D-galactose and β-D-N-acetylgalactosamine are components of blood group antigens. Deficient conversion causes galactosaemia (mental retardation, cataracts, early death if untreated).
RIBOSE5-carbon sugar — a component of RNA and coenzymes. 2-Deoxyribose (OH at C-2 replaced by H) is the sugar of DNA.
2–10 sugar units
Disaccharides — two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond — are the simplest oligosaccharides.
The major disaccharides

c: Component of malt; formed from starch by diastase during germination; fermented by yeast in brewing beer.
Main carbohydrate in milk; hydrolysed by lactase; deficiency causes lactose intolerance.
Table sugar, produced by plants; hydrolysed by sucrase; has no reducing end (both anomeric carbons are joined).
Formed at the branch points of starch/glycogen.

blocks.x: Every disaccharide except sucrose retains one free anomeric carbon — the reducing end — which is why sucrose is classed as a non-reducing sugar.
Maltose
Glucose-α-1,4-glucose, a component of malt. Diastase, produced during germination, catalyses the hydrolysis of starch to maltose, which is then fermented by yeast — crucial to the brewing of beer.
Lactose

Galactose-β-1,4-glucose, the main carbohydrate in milk, critical for nutrition in early mammalian life. It cannot be absorbed directly into the bloodstream — it must first be broken down into galactose and glucose by lactase.

People who lack lactase cannot hydrolyse lactose (lactose intolerance). Undigested lactose remains in the intestinal tract, causing cramping and diarrhoea that can lead to dehydration; intestinal bacteria metabolise it, releasing organic acids and CO2. Effects are avoided by excluding milk/milk products, or by taking lactase tablets with dairy foods.
Sucrose

Glucose-α-1,2-fructose, produced by many higher plants via photosynthesis; commonly known as table sugar. It cannot be absorbed directly and is hydrolysed by sucrase in the human intestine into glucose and fructose.

In plants it is water-soluble and easily transported through the plant circulatory system. High sucrose concentration produces high osmotic pressure that bars microbial growth, so it is used as a preservative and sweetener. Because sucrose supplies "empty calories" (no vitamins or minerals), research links high sucrose consumption to dental caries, obesity, diabetes, NAFLD and cardiovascular disease.
Oligosaccharides as drug components
Oligosaccharides occur widely as components of drugs — for example Bleomycin A2, an antitumor agent used clinically against specific tumours, and Streptomycin, a broad-spectrum antibiotic.
>10 sugar units (glycans)
Polysaccharides serve two major functions: as stores of energy, and as providers of physical structure and strength to organisms.
Homo- vs. heteropolysaccharides
Homopolysaccharides (Homoglycan)
Built from one kind of monosaccharide. Named by suffix "-an": glucans (glucose), mannans (mannose), galacturonans (galactose), arabinans (arabinose).
Heteropolysaccharides (Heteroglycan)
Built from more than one kind of monosaccharide, e.g. peptidoglycan and lipopolysaccharide of bacterial cell walls.
Stores of energy — starch & glycogen

items: Amylose (10–30% of starch): unbranched chain of glucose in α(1→4) linkages; adopts a helical conformation in water. Iodine inserts into the helix to give the characteristic, diagnostic blue colour of the starch–iodine test.
Amylopectin (70–90% of starch): α(1→4)-linked chains with α(1→6) branch points roughly every 12–30 residues.

Digestion: salivary α-amylase (endoamylase, mouth, splits α(1→4) only, inactivated by stomach acid) → pancreatic α-amylase (endoamylase, small intestine) → β-amylase (exoamylase, found only in some plants/microbes) → α(1→6)-glucosidase (cleaves the branch points). Cooked starch is more digestible because heating swells the granules.

Split into monosaccharides: starch phosphorylase performs stepwise phosphorolytic cleavage from the non-reducing end, releasing α-D-glucose-1-phosphate, which feeds glycolytic pathways to produce ATP.

blocks.x: Glycogen is the key form of stored polysaccharide in animals — mainly in the liver (about 10% of liver mass) and skeletal muscle (1–2% of muscle mass). Liver glycogen is highly branched, with α(1→6) branch points every 8–12 residues — more frequent branching than starch.
Hydrolysis of glycogen proceeds two ways: amylases yield glucose + maltose, while glycogen phosphorylase yields glucose-1-phosphate.
A polysaccharide of D-glucose with a main chain of α(1→6) linkages and branches at 1→2, 1→3 or 1→4. Cross-linked with epichlorohydrin, dextran forms the chromatography gel media Sephadex and Bio-Gel.
Physical structure & strength — cellulose & more

items: A structural, homopolymer of D-glucose linked by β(1→4) glycosidic bonds, found in the cell walls of nearly all plants.
Adopts an extended conformation (unlike starch's helical shape); glucose units flip and form stable inter- and intrachain hydrogen bonds.

The most abundant polysaccharide, and indeed the most abundant organic molecule in the world. Cellulose typically contains about 3,000 glucose units, but the alga Valonia produces cellulose with 26,000 glucose units.

Unlike glycogen, amylose and amylopectin, humans cannot digest cellulose because we cannot synthesise cellulase. Termites, cows and goats can digest cellulose (via symbiotic organisms). Cellulose is hydrolysed by cellulase and β-glucosidase.

Peptidoglycan: a strong, protective peptide-polysaccharide layer of bacteria, built from alternating N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid, cross-linked through a tetrapeptide (L-Ala–D-Glu–L-Lys–D-Ala). Gram-positive bacteria have thick peptidoglycan layers (~25 nm) cross-linked by a pentaglycine bridge; Gram-negative bacteria have a thin, single peptidoglycan layer (2–3 nm) with direct cross-links, sandwiched between inner and outer lipid bilayer membranes.

Lipopolysaccharide (LPS): found only in Gram-negative bacteria, anchored in the outer membrane; built from a core oligosaccharide (heptose, KDO, NAG) plus a repeating O-antigen chain (mannose, rhamnose, abequose, D-galactose).

blocks.x: Further structural polysaccharides

c: Fungal cell walls; exoskeletons of crustaceans and insects
Marine red algae; forms a double helix

blocks.x: Complexes & laboratory identification
Carbohydrates conjugate with proteins to form glycoproteins and proteoglycans, and can be identified in the lab by a set of characteristic colour reactions.
Glycoproteins & proteoglycans
Glycoproteins
Carbohydrate groups link to polypeptide chains, including structural proteins, enzymes, membrane receptors, transport proteins and immunoglobulins.
O-linked saccharides: attach to the –OH of Ser, Thr or hydroxylysine. N-linked saccharides: attach to the amide (N) of asparagine.
Proteoglycans
A family of glycoproteins whose carbohydrate moieties are predominantly glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), O-linked to Ser-Gly. Often soluble and located in the extracellular matrix.
Proteoglycans modulate cell growth processes and are responsible for the flexibility and resilience of cartilage tissue in the body (e.g. versican, decorin, syndecan, cartilage proteoglycan).
Tests for carbohydrates

c: Conc. H2SO4 dehydrates sugars to furfural (from pentoses) or hydroxymethylfurfural (from hexoses), which condenses with α-naphthol → purple (violet-red) ring.
Pentoses form furfural in conc. HCl, which condenses with orcinol + Fe3+ → green/blue-green complex, soluble in butanol.
Ketoses dehydrate faster with acid to give furfural derivatives that condense with resorcinol → cherry-red complex quickly; aldoses give a brownish colour, more slowly.
Reducing sugars reduce Cu2+ to Cu+ in Benedict's reagent (cupric sulphate, sodium carbonate, sodium citrate) → colour shifts green → dark red/rusty brown with the amount of sugar.

Fehling's solution A (aqueous copper sulphate) + solution B (alkaline sodium potassium tartrate, the chelating agent) mixed 1:1 → brick-red precipitate, like Benedict's, but Benedict's reagent is more stable than Fehling's.
Reduction of copper(II) acetate to copper(I) oxide (Cu2O) → brick-red precipitate, faster for monosaccharides; disaccharides may react, but much more slowly.
